Article Title: At 18, Salman Khan lost his father, drove taxi for months before becoming an Army man and now an Asian Games rowing medallist
Article Text:
Indian rowers Satnam Singh and Salman Khan pose with their bronze medal (PTI Photo)

Salman lost his father at 18

A friend's advice changed his life

How Salman became a rower

The turning point

From national gold to international success

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

From driving a cab to wearing the India jersey

For rower Salman Khan , winning an Asian Games medal is the latest chapter in a journey that began with family responsibilities, financial struggles and a job as a cab driver.The Indian rower won the bronze medal in the men's double sculls event alongside teammate Satnam Singh at the Asian Games 2026 on Thursday. The Indian pair stayed in second place until the 1,500m mark before slipping to third in the final 500m. They finished the race in 6:13.25 at the Nagaragawa International Regatta Course.China's Yi Xudi and Yide Nie won gold with a timing of 6:09.37, while Uzbekistan's Pavel Sorin and Mekhrojbek Mamatkulov took silver in 6:10.49.For Salman, the medal has come after years of hard work and a life that could have taken a very different path.Salman was born in Pure Dhingai in Amethi district of Uttar Pradesh. His father, Mohammed Kasim Khan, worked in truck-body construction in Tauru, Haryana, where Salman completed his schooling.He was the eldest of four brothers and two sisters. When his father died of dengue, Salman was just 18 years old.With his younger siblings still studying, the responsibility of supporting the family fell on him. His dream of joining the Army had to take a backseat as earning a livelihood became his priority.Salman started driving an Uber cab in Delhi. He worked day and night to keep his family going.Salman had not given up completely on his Army dream. One day, while resting after a shift, a close friend reminded him that his height and physical build could help him in the Army. That advice pushed him to try again.He handed over the cab to another driver and spent four months preparing through hard running and training. He cleared the recruitment rally, medical and written examinations.In September 2018, he joined the Bombay Engineer Group (BEG), Kirkee, Pune.At the training centre, coaches noticed Salman's height and physique and introduced him to rowing. He knew nothing about the sport and initially had no interest in taking it up. With his family's financial situation, sport was not something he thought he could pursue.He refused several times. But the coaches continued to push him and eventually put him in a boat. They saw potential in him and began training him seriously.Salman's first inter-centre regatta gave him the first sign that he could make something out of rowing. He won a silver medal, which gave him confidence.The next major step came in 2021 when Salman cleared the ergometer benchmarks and was selected for the Army Rowing Node at CME Pune. Training alongside some of India's best rowers changed his outlook.What had started as a sport he did not even want to take up became something he wanted to pursue professionally.Salman began to believe that rowing could help him win medals for India.Salman's progress continued over the next few years. At the 36th National Games in Gujarat in 2022, he won gold. At the 2023 Senior Nationals, he won gold in the single sculls against Olympian Dattu Bhokanal. That performance helped him earn a place in the India camp.In 2024, Salman won his first international gold at the Asian Rowing Cup in South Korea with Nitin Deol. That victory also earned him a promotion to Naib Subedar in the Indian Army.He followed it with a silver at the 2025 Australian Rowing Championships and another silver at the 2025 Asian Rowing Championships.Those performances helped him secure his place in India's Asian Games squad.For Salman, representing India carries a special meaning because of where his journey started. He came from a village background and had to take responsibility for his family at a very young age.His mother, Jabrun Nisha, remained a major source of strength for him, while his wife, Sahiba Khatoon, supported him throughout his journey.His coaches and support staff also played a major role in keeping him on the rowing path, particularly during periods when he lost interest in the sport.At the Army Rowing Node, officers and coaches helped him regain his focus and develop as an athlete.Salman's journey from Amethi to the Indian Army, and from an unfamiliar boat to an Asian Games medal, has been built over years of perseverance, discipline and the support of his family, coaches and teammates.

The indian pair stayed in second place until the 1,500m mark before slipping to third in the final 500m. China's yi xudi and yide nie won gold with a timing of 6:09.37. Uzbekistan's pavel sorin and mekhrojbek mamatkulov took silver in 6:10.49.

Article Title: Roshibina Devi: From missing India's original squad to making history with silver, Roshibina Devi becomes first Indian woman to win three successive Asian Games medals
Article Text:
India's Roshibina Devi Naorem holds the silver medal after the Women's 60kg Wushu final match during the 20th Asian Games. (PTI Photo)

From controversy to the podium

Little time to prepare

India's Naorem Roshibina Devi, blue, competes against China's Zhang Xiaoyu in the in the Women's 60kg Wushu match final (PTI Photo)

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Naorem Roshibina Devi's Asian Games journey began with uncertainty but ended with another medal. The 25-year-old Manipuri wushu player won silver in the women's 60kg Sanda category after losing 0-2 to China's Zhang Xiaoyu in the final at the Aichi Prefectural Martial Arts Hall on Thursday.With the silver, Roshibina became the first Indian woman to win three successive Asian Games medals in wushu, following her bronze at Jakarta 2018 and silver at Hangzhou 2023.Roshibina was not part of India's original squad after losing the selection trial to Divyanshi Choudhary in June. Divyanshi was initially selected but was later withdrawn after the Wushu Association of India said an MRI showed a partial high-grade ACL tear.Divyanshi had alleged that she was being mentally and physically harassed and claimed Roshibina had been involved. The WAI rejected the allegations and said the squad change was made on medical grounds. The Sports Ministry subsequently approved Roshibina as the replacement.Roshibina, who learnt about her inclusion around September 10, said she wanted to move on from the controversy."What happened was not because of me. It was the federation's decision.Whatever decision the federation (Wushu Association of India) took, I think it was a good decision," she said."I will ignore it (the accusation). I just want to focus on my goal."Roshibina had been out of the national camp for around one-and-a-half months after losing the trials and travelled directly from Manipur after being recalled."There was a lot of disturbance when I came here for the Asian Games. I did not get much time to prepare. If I had more time, I would have done better," she said.Her coach Amit Pal also pointed to the lack of preparation, saying Roshibina had only limited training after being named in the team on September 10.Despite that, she defeated Bangladesh's Shika Khatun in the pre-quarterfinals and Macao, China's Chu Man Sin 5-0 in the quarterfinals before securing another Asian Games medal.Roshibina could not match Zhang's aggression and technical superiority in the gold-medal bout. The Chinese fighter won both rounds unanimously, with all five judges awarding her 5-0 decisions.Zhang dominated the scoring in both rounds, particularly with her side-kicks."She (Chinese player) is a new player, I have not fought against her. She was good in her side kicks. I also tried to defend. I tried to throw her, but she did better," Roshibina said.The silver left her disappointed at missing gold."I have won silver earlier and this time also, I could win only silver. I could not give the gold medal to the Indian people. I could not give what everyone wanted," she said.Born in Kwasiphai Mayai Leikai in Manipur's Bishnupur district, Roshibina's journey has also involved considerable family sacrifice, with her farmer father Naorem Damu Singh selling a piece of land to fund her training and travel in the early years.Now, with three successive Asian Games medals, Roshibina has another target."I want to inspire all the players. I want to be like them. I will do my best in the upcoming Games."
Article Summary: Naorem roshibina devi won silver in the women's 60kg sanda category. She lost 0-2 to china's zhang xiaoyu in the final at the aichi prefectural martial arts hall on thursday. The 25-year-old manipuri wushu player won bronze at jakarta 2018 and silver at hangzhou 2023.

Article Title: Chess Olympiad Round 7: India's chances of gold get bleaker despite win in open; women still in hunt
Article Text:
Nihal Sarin and Savitha Shri (Photo by Rafal Oleksiewicz and Michal Walusza for FIDE)

Savitha Shri , a potent force for India at 2026 Chess Olympiad

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

NEW DELHI: India will look back at Nihal Sarin's loss before the rest day and wonder what might have happened had he taken a few more minutes — he had plenty of time on the clock, more than enough to have avoided the queen blunder that cost India their Round 6 match against Uzbekistan on Monday. When the players returned to the board for Round 7 in Samarkand on Wednesday, following Tuesday's rest day, the overall picture in the race for gold remained largely unchanged.Another hope of an Uzbek slip-up, this time at the hands of an in-form Chinese team, evaporated as the hosts won 3-1, moving a step closer to another coveted Chess Olympiad title. India's open team also won on the day, though not as comfortably as the Uzbeks.India's opponents were England, and with Dommaraju Gukesh and Rameshbabu Praggnanandhaa having already wrapped up wins on their boards, the team's fate no longer rested on Nihal, which was just as well, because he lost again on Board 3, this time in a marathon 88-move battle against Luke McShane.McShane, playing white, produced a stubborn, fighting performance against the higher-rated Nihal.The Englishman took the initiative early, pushing pawns on both the queenside and kingside, while Nihal hit back with active piece play and a dangerous-looking attack on White's king.The position stayed unresolved for a long time, and by the time both players were down to their final seconds on the clock, the game had turned into a test of nerve as much as calculation.McShane held firm, found the right defensive moves under pressure, and gradually turned his rooks into the more active pieces on the board.The turning point came with 66.Re8, forcing off a pair of rooks and steering the game into a simplified endgame. This was exactly the kind of position where McShane's advanced f-pawn and increasingly active king took over.From there, he picked off Nihal's pawns one by one, and after nearly seven hours of play,Nihal resigned on move 88.It left Nihal with back-to-back individual losses at a tournament where he had otherwise been one of India's most reliable performers.India closed out the England match 2.5-1.5, with wins from Praggnanandhaa and Gukesh outweighing Nihal's loss and Arjun Erigaisi's draw.It keeps India firmly in the group chasing Uzbekistan, who remain the only team with a perfect record after seven rounds, a gap that will be hard to close with just four rounds left.If the open section's gold hopes are fading, India's women's team gave every reason to believe theirs are still very much alive, and 19-year-old Savitha Shri has been a big part of why.The Chennai-born player has now played six games at this Olympiad and won every single one, and Wednesday's win over Germany's Lara Schulze followed the same pattern.After a fairly balanced opening, Savitha. with the Whites, gradually seized control with active piece play and mounting pressure on the kingside.The position turned complicated around the 34th move, when she allowed a trade of pieces that led into a tricky rook-and-knight endgame, one she navigated calmly even as Schulze fell into serious time trouble.Savitha's rook grew increasingly active from there, picking off pawns and creating threats on both sides of the board, and though Schulze tried to fight back, Savitha never let her king come under real danger.In a phase that tested patience above all else, with both players short on time, Savitha pushed her kingside pawns forward until 88.g6+ proved decisive, leaving Schulze unable to save her rook.It capped a near-90-move grind with a well-earned win and helped India rout Germany 3.5-0.5, with Koneru Humpy and Divya Deshmukh also winning their games and Vaishali Rameshbabu drawing on Board 2.ALSO READ: Juggling Chess Olympiad prep and a commentary gig in India: The other side of USA's only female GM Irina Krush With India's open team hoping now for an unlikely Uzbek slip, they face Azerbaijan in Round 8 on Thursday. The women's team, who still hold better medal chances than their male counterparts on current form, take on Kazakhstan.
Article Summary: Nihal sarin loses again on board 3, this time in a marathon 88-move battle against luke mcshane. 19-year-old savitha shri has now played six games at this olympiad and won every single one, and wednesday's win over germany's lara schulze followed the same pattern.

Article Title: Mirabai Chanu’s first coach sees another Olympic medal after elusive Asian Games silver
Article Text:
Mirabai Chanu during a training session ahead of the Asian Games and (pic right) with coach S Brojendro Singh after winning the gold medal at 2018 Commonwealth Games

TOI

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

When a young Mirabai Chanu first walked into the weightlifting centre at Khuman Lampak in Imphal in 2006, there was little to suggest she would one day become India’s most decorated weightlifter.Twenty years later, after Mirabai clinched a silver medal in the women’s 49kg category at the Asian Games , her first-ever medal at the continental showpiece, her former coach S Brojendro Singh believes she is still not done.“I am very happy for her. She already has an Olympic medal, and I believe she will win another Olympic medal as well,” Singh told. “Now that she has won an Asian Games medal, I believe she can win a medal in Los Angeles, too.”Singh coached Mirabai at the state sports academy at Khuman Lampak Main Stadium from 2006 to 2011, overseeing the now 32-year-old lifter’s formative years in the sport. Those early days, he recalled, were marked by a work ethic that set her apart from her peers.“Whatever she was told to do, she did it. She never missed any instruction. If we asked her to do something, she would complete it exactly as told,” said Singh, who has been coaching at the academy since 2004.“That discipline was different. She was also fearless and never shied away from a challenge.”Not everything was smooth at the beginning. Singh remembered a period when the youngster stopped attending training sessions.“She was absent for almost a month early in 2007. I got worried and went straight to her home. Later, I found out that she had chickenpox. Once she recovered, she returned and continued training,” said the coach, who has trained numerous other international medallists, including Rishikanta Singh and Nirupama Devi.Asked if he had spotted signs of greatness in the teenager, Singh pointed not to extraordinary physical attributes but to her attitude. “Her dedication was exceptional. She listened, she worked hard and she was never afraid. Those qualities made her different from the others,” he said.Mirabai’s rise from Khuman Lampak to the Olympic podium has also inspired a generation of weightlifters in Manipur, but Singh believes athletes with her combination of talent, discipline and determination are rare.“In all my years as a coach, I have not seen another weightlifter quite like Mirabai,” he said. “Many athletes look up to her, but finding someone with her qualities is very difficult.”Having won Olympic silver in Tokyo and now added an elusive Asian Games medal to her collection, after also securing her third Commonwealth Games gold medal, Mirabai may have achieved almost everything in the sport. Yet, if her first coach is to be believed, the story is far from over.“She still has a lot to achieve,” Singh said. “I am confident there is more to come from her.”Long before the Olympic medal, the world title and the Asian Games silver, Mirabai’s days revolved around hitching rides on passing trucks to travel from her village to Imphal for training and helping her family by collecting firewood and carrying water uphill in the hills of Manipur.Two decades on, the resilience forged during those years continues to power one of India’s greatest sporting careers and, if her first coach is right, perhaps another Olympic medal run as well.
Article Summary: Mirabai chanu won silver in the women's 49kg category at the asian games. It was her first-ever medal at the continental showpiece. Her former coach s brojendro singh believes she is still not done. Singh coached mirabai at the state sports academy at khuman lampak main stadium.

Article Title: Cristiano Ronaldo and Georgina Rodríguez bought a €25 million plot on Dubai’s ‘Billionaire Island’ to build a custom mansion, after leasing their Madrid villa for €10,000 a month
Article Text:

Why Did Cristiano Ronaldo And Georgina Rodríguez Lease Their Madrid Villa For €10,000 A Month

Cristiano Ronaldo and Georgina Rodríguez expanded their property portfolio in 2024 with a €25 million land purchase on Dubai’s Jumeirah Bay Island, a luxury development often called “Billionaire Island”. The couple planned to build a private mansion on the waterfront plot as Ronaldo continued his career with Saudi Pro League club Al-Nassr. The purchase came after they had put their Madrid home in La Finca up for rent for €10,000 a month in 2023. The Dubai deal gave the family a permanent property base in the Gulf while adding another major asset to Ronaldo’s international real estate portfolio.Ronaldo and Rodríguez reportedly paid €25 million (£21 million/$27 million) for the Dubai plot in 2024. The land is on Jumeirah Bay Island, a man-made island shaped roughly like a seahorse and located off Dubai’s coast.The island is known for its small number of high-end homes and its location close to some of Dubai’s luxury hotels and facilities. It is connected to the mainland by a private bridge and is home to the Bulgari Resort and Bulgari Yacht Club.ge.globo reported in June 2024 that the couple had completed the purchase and planned to build a mansion for themselves and their five children.The report said the property was expected to be ready by the end of December that year.The purchase also made sense geographically for Ronaldo. His professional life had moved to Saudi Arabia after joining Al-Nassr, while Dubai offered a nearby base for the family and their wider business interests.The island’s appeal is not simply its location. Jumeirah Bay Island has become one of Dubai’s most exclusive residential areas, with a limited number of waterfront properties. Khaleej Times reported that the island has 124 sea-facing villas across the development, highlighting how limited the residential supply is.Instead of purchasing a finished house, Ronaldo and Rodríguez planned a home around their own requirements. Reports in 2024 linked the project to Palace Luxury Living, a UAE luxury property company.The biggest difference is that the Dubai home was planned as a private family residence rather than simply another investment property. Ronaldo and Rodríguez have five children, so the layout needed to work for a large family as well as their staff.Details reported about the planned property have included large living areas, private bedrooms, fitness facilities and outdoor spaces facing the water. The waterfront setting also gives the family direct access to the Dubai coastline.Rodríguez has also shown a strong interest in the design of the couple’s homes. Their previous residences have featured modern interiors, large open areas, marble surfaces and extensive outdoor spaces.That approach is easy to understand when looking at the size of the family’s other homes. Ronaldo’s properties have often been designed around football, fitness, privacy and family life rather than simply being luxury addresses.The Dubai mansion therefore fits into a pattern already seen across the couple’s property portfolio: large spaces, private facilities and enough room for family life without giving up the features expected from a high-end home.Long before Dubai became part of their property story, Rodríguez had already experienced what it was like to live in one of Ronaldo’s unusually large homes.The couple’s Madrid residence is located in La Finca, an exclusive residential development in Pozuelo de Alarcón. Ronaldo bought the property in 2010 for around €5 million while he was playing for Real Madrid.The home later became closely associated with Rodríguez through her Netflix series. When she first moved into Ronaldo’s home, she admitted that its size made it difficult for her to find her way around.“The first time I came to Cristiano’s house, well I’d get lost,” Rodríguez revealed in her hit Netflix docuseries I Am Georgina. “I’d want to go to the kitchen to get water and I’d no idea where to go. Sometimes it would take me half an hour to get to the living room because I didn’t know the way back. Since I was a kid I had been so used to living in really small apartments”.She later said it took about six months before she knew the house properly.The Madrid property was designed by architect Joaquín Torres and has been reported as having seven bedrooms and nine bathrooms, along with indoor and outdoor pools and a gym. Ronaldo also added personal touches, including CR7-branded door handles.The scale of the property became even more notable after the couple decided they no longer needed to keep it solely as their family home.After Ronaldo left Real Madrid and later moved through Juventus and Manchester United before joining Al-Nassr, his time in Madrid became much more limited. In 2023, the couple put the La Finca property on the rental market for €10,000 a month.La Vanguardia reported that the house had been Ronaldo’s Madrid home during his Real Madrid years and was later offered for rent at that monthly price. The report also noted that the property was offered furnished.The decision meant the couple could keep the Madrid property instead of selling it while no longer using it as their main home.Reports described the residence as a large multi-level property with several bedrooms, bathrooms, a gym and swimming pools. Much of the furniture and decoration stayed in the house, allowing a tenant to move into the property without having to furnish it from scratch.The Dubai purchase then added a very different kind of property to their portfolio. Madrid represented Ronaldo’s long connection with Spain and his Real Madrid years. Jumeirah Bay, meanwhile, placed the family closer to his current life in the Gulf.The couple’s wider property holdings also include homes in Portugal and Spain, while Ronaldo’s business interests extend into the hotel industry through the Pestana CR7 brand.For Ronaldo and Rodríguez, the €25 million Jumeirah Bay plot was therefore more than another expensive address. It marked the move from having a temporary base in the Middle East to building a home designed specifically for their family there.
Article Summary: Cristiano ronaldo and georgina rodríguez bought a €25 million plot on dubai’s ‘billionaire island’ to build a custom mansion. The purchase came after they had put their madrid home in la finca up for rent for €10,000 a month in 2023. The couple planned to build the private mansion on the waterfront plot as ronaldo continued his career with saudi pro league club al-nassr.

Article Title: Unplayed Mongolia fixture denies India shot at historic Asian Games esports medal
Article Text:
India eye record medals at Asian Games 2026

New Delhi:

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

India’s hopes of securing a historic esports medal at the Asian Games in Japan suffered a setback after an unplayed eFootball fixture against Mongolia was recorded as a forfeit win, leaving India without the goal difference it needed to remain in contention for the knockout stage.India’s eFootball pair of Chinmay Sahoo and Danial Patel, coached by Saksham Rattan, had earlier drawn 0-0 against Uzbekistan’s Abubakir Iminjonov and Farrukh Mirkhamitov. With India needing a win in its next Group F fixture, Mongolia’s Munkh-Ochir Batmanlai and Khantamir Munkh-Orgil failed to report to the Call Room within the stipulated time. India was subsequently awarded a 0-0 forfeit victory.However, Uzbekistan defeated Mongolia 2-0 across the console and mobile matches and finished top of Group F. With only the group winner advancing directly to the quarterfinals, India’s campaign ended despite its awarded victory.The Esports Federation of India (ESFI) has raised concerns over the circumstances surrounding the fixture and the subsequent qualification calculations. The federation said India was denied the opportunity to actually play Mongolia, score goals and improve its goal difference, which it says was relevant to determining qualification among the teams.According to ESFI, Uzbekistan was able to play its fixture against Mongolia and subsequently benefited from the resulting goal difference before eventually winning the bronze medal. ESFI has questioned whether recording no goal difference for India’s forfeited match created an unequal sporting opportunity.The federation also cited a series of technical and scheduling disruptions. Matches scheduled for 9am reportedly began only after 11.30am due to problems with an organiser-provided playing device. The Uzbekistan-Mongolia fixture, scheduled for around 3pm, reportedly started at approximately 5pm Japan time, affecting the timing of the India-Mongolia encounter.ESFI further alleged that Mongolia had not been adequately briefed about the required Call Room reporting time and that its team manager was unable to leave the preceding match to complete the reporting process for the next fixture.The federation said India’s subsequent request for a review by the Olympic Council of Asia, the Esports Organising Committee and competition management went unacknowledged. ESFI also alleged that India was not given adequate clarity on the applicable rules within the stipulated 15-minute window to lodge a formal protest.India sought clarification on the regulatory basis for recording no goal difference in forfeited matches, the use of average points and average goal difference for ranking, the complete qualification calculations and when the ranking methodology was formally communicated to participating teams.ESFI has called for a transparent review, a written response and appropriate corrective action, while reaffirming its respect for competition rules and technical officials.India’s 15-member esports contingent is competing across four disciplines: eFootball, Puyo Puyo Champions, Pokémon UNITE and League of Legends.
Article Summary: India’s hopes of securing a historic esports medal at the asian games suffered a setback. An unplayed efootball fixture against mongolia was recorded as a forfeit win, leaving india without the goal difference it needed to remain in contention for the knockout stage.

Article Title: From missing Hangzhou to silver in Nagoya: Mirabai Chanu’s Asian Games redemption
Article Text:
Mirabai Chanu (PTI Photo)

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Nagoya: Two hundred and sixty-four grams.That was all it took to complete Mirabai Chanu ’s collection of heavyweight medals.The silver medallion awarded at Aichi-Nagoya weighs 264gm, but for Mirabai it could well be worth its weight in gold.Six years ago, it was also in Japan that Mirabai won an Olympic silver at the Tokyo Games. In the land of the rising sun, she delivered again, this time in a statement of persistence and resilience.At the Nagoya City Trade and Industry Centre here on Wednesday, the 32-year-old ended India’s 28-year wait for an Asian Games weightlifting medal, winning silver and, in the process, finally adding a continental medal to her cabinet.“I feel very good. This Asian Games medal was my dream and finally I got a silver medal. Since I stepped into the elite level, this has been my dream,” gushed Mirabai after her medal-winning performance.Competing in the 49kg category, the lifter, who wore tricolour hair ties, totalled 198kg (87kg in snatch + 111kg in clean and jerk) to finish behind defending champion Ri Song-gum. The North Korean was in another stratosphere altogether, lifting a world-record 215kg (94+121), a full 17kg more than the Indian.Indonesia’s Luluk Diana Tri Wijayana took bronze with 191kg (88+103).Mirabai was assured in the snatch, clearing 83kg, 85kg and 87kg without much fuss. She trailed Ri and Luluk going into the clean and jerk, but successfully negotiated 107kg and 111kg to secure silver.Asked why the continental medal was her dream and not the Olympic silverware which she already possessed, Mirabai said, “Competition in Asian weightlifting is very strong with Korea, China etc. I believe that medals in Asian Games are equal to the ones won at the Olympics. In fact, I feel the competition at the Asian Games is tougher than the Olympics.”For an athlete who had dreamed of an Asian Games podium for years, the medal was also a measure of redemption.Mirabai missed the 2018 edition because of a back injury. In Hangzhou three years ago, a hip and thigh injury hampered her during her final attempt and left her fourth.Earlier this year, a lingering shoulder injury had cast another shadow over her season. But Mirabai put that behind her by winning gold at the Glasgow Commonwealth Games.Her resilience has deep roots.Born in Nongpok Kakching in southeastern Manipur, Mirabai grew up in a landscape that is picturesque and also steeped in history and identity. The region, known for landmarks such as Kakching Garden and the People’s Museum, has also witnessed the imprint of World War II, with Langol Peak serving as a campsite for Allied forces. From that landscape emerged an athlete who has repeatedly had to rise after setbacks.If age and injuries threatened to slow her down, Mirabai had a support system that refused to let that happen. While coach Vijay Sharma took care of her training, American strength and conditioning coach Dr Aaron Horschig monitored her fitness and recovery. A nutritionist, meanwhile, ensured she stayed on top of her weight.The work that went into the medal, she said, was immense.“A lot of work. After the Commonwealth Games, there was very little time. At the same time, I had to control my weight at 48kg (for the CWG). It was very difficult for me to control my weight,” explained the Padma Shri awardee.One of the most keenly watched Indian athletes at the Games, Mirabai also had to contend with the weight of expectation.“There is pressure, but I also have confidence. The whole world has had hopes of me winning a medal. I draw strength from the fact that people think positively about me and pray for me so much. That said, the pressure of not delivering is also there,” she said.With the Asian Games medal finally ticked off her bucket list, attention inevitably turns to another question: is a fourth Olympic appearance at the 2028 Los Angeles Games on the horizon?“We haven’t finalised anything yet. But we will try. Qualifying starts in Dec. But for now, I will enjoy it,” she signed off.
Article Summary: Mirabai chanu won silver in the 49kg category at the asian games. The 32-year-old ended india’s 28-year wait for an asian games medal. She finished behind defending champion ri song-gum of north korea.

Article Title: ​At 90, former paratrooper Ian Winship runs 10K in about an hour with daughter and grandson, setting a world-best time for his age
Article Text:
Pic credit: Gibson Digital/North Lanarkshire Council

Age, just a number

Pic credit: Gibson Digital/North Lanarkshire Council

3 generations in motion

Pic credit: Gibson Digital/North Lanarkshire Council

Ian Winship, a 90-year-old runner from North Lanarkshire, has completed a 10-kilometre race in about 1 hour, 4 minutes and 37 seconds, setting what is believed to be a world-best time for his age group. On 13 September, the former paratrooper completed the Cumbernauld 10K run. "I stood greetin'," the former paratrooper told the BBC, his disbelief still evident.It's easy to understand why. Winship wasn't chasing records when he started that morning. He was doing what he does most days: running. The world-best time in the M90 category came out of the blue. “It's just unbelievable. Cumbernauld might be famous now because of me.”Scottish Athletics confirmed the achievement is considered a ‘world best’ rather than a ‘world record’, as non-professional road races lack the precision required for official ratification. But there are simply no reports of anyone older achieving a faster time.Ian Winship, who hails from Cumberland, revealed the secret behind the record. He gets up each morning, fetches his paper, gets his coffee, and walks.Not around the block, but for miles. Most days, he hits 20,000 steps. Long stretches through Cumbernauld are a regimen he religiously follows to keep himself fit.Winship understands what most people don’t. “I've got a purpose, I want to stay alive. If I sit in the house I'll vegetate. I must meet people.” So he walks and continues to share ties with the community. It’s the perspective of someone who spent his younger years as a paratrooper, jumping into Egypt near Port Said during the Suez Crisis in 1956, and later became a steeplejack. Motion was always the job. Now it's the medicine.For him, what really works is consistency. He does not have a fancy training plan or gym membership. But every morning he wakes up and gets moving. His next challenge is to ‘live to 100’.When Winship completed the race, he was a little ‘wobbly’, so the paramedics offered him a wheelchair. But the 90-year-old turned it down immediately.Winship had the best company in the race. The nonagenarian ran this race alongside his daughter, Fiona Fleming, and grandson Kyle Fleming, 26, who came third. It wasn't their first time making the race a family affair at Cumbernauld. But the grandfather's performance still caught them off guard.Kyle is proud of his grandpa. “He gets up every morning, goes to get his paper, goes to get his coffee. He does 20,000 steps a day. It's incredible,” he told the broadcaster."I run because it keeps me sane, keeps me fit and it keeps me out of trouble,” Winship always told his family.For Kyle, watching his grandpa was inspiration enough. "That's always stuck with me. Every time I see him running, that's what I think about. He lost his wife years ago, and I think it just keeps him going."Meanwhile, Scottish Athletics said Winship's achievement is considered a ‘world best’ in the M90 category. A spokesperson for the body said they were "delighted to hear of Ian's great run". "Athletics can be for life if that's what you want and performances like this one by Ian at 90 really are inspirational."Kenneth Duffy, provost of North Lanarkshire, called him ‘a hero’. "My huge congratulations to Ian on his outstanding achievement at this year's Cumbernauld 10K event. What a hero he is! I'm sure everyone will be inspired by his determination, commitment and enthusiasm. To complete a 10K at 90 years of age is a remarkable accomplishment, let alone complete it in such an impressive time."Geraldine Woods, convener of communities at the council, also lauded Winship’s achievement. "Ian's performance at this year's event, along with his dedication and positive attitude, is an inspiration to people of all ages."
Article Summary: Ian winship, a 90-year-old runner from north lanarkshire, has completed a 10-kilometre race in about 1 hour, 4 minutes and 37 seconds. The former paratrooper completed the cumbernauld 10k run on 13 september. Scottish athletics said winship's achievement is considered a 'world best' in the m90 category.

Article Title: In 2007, a rare Atari game surfaced at a garage sale; 19 years later, it sold with its original cassette for $6,562.50
Article Text:
Representative Image of the Atari 2600 game Red Sea Crossing with its cartridge, coloring book, and audiocassette, showcasing Christian themes (AI Generated)

The Atari game placed players in the story of Moses

Its only known advertisement appeared in Christianity Today

A garage-sale discovery brought the game back into view

The cassette made the 2026 auction unusual

Red Sea Crossing sold for $6,562.50

A rare Christian-themed Atari 2600 game that surfaced at a garage sale in 2007 has sold at auction for $6,562.50. Red Sea Crossing, released through mail order in 1983, was offered by Heritage Auctions with an accompanying audiocassette. The sale marked the first time the cassette itself had been presented at auction, according to the auction house. Steve Schustack created the game and takes its inspiration from the biblical story of Moses parting the Red Sea. Players guide Moses between walls of water while avoiding obstacles and the pursuing Egyptian army. The cartridge was sold at Heritage Auctions’ June 12–13, 2026 Video Games Signature Auction, where it was listed as lot 28003.Red Sea Crossing was released for the Atari 2600 in 1983 by Inspirational Video Concepts. Unlike many commercial console games of the period, it was not distributed through ordinary retail channels. Heritage describes it as a mail-order release with a Christian theme. The gameplay centres on Moses crossing the Red Sea. The player must guide him between the parted waters while avoiding hazards including seaweed, giant clams and the Egyptian army.The game also includes a fish that acts as a time limit, requiring players to reach the end of the screen before it catches up with Moses. The package was unusual in another respect. Instead of being accompanied only by a conventional instruction manual, the game was originally sold with a colouring book and an explanatory audiocassette connected to the story of the Exodus. Heritage identifies the cassette as being narrated by Dale Evans Rogers.The game’s limited distribution has contributed to its rarity. Heritage states that its only marketing was an advertisement in the October 7, 1983 issue of Christianity Today. The advertisement offered the game by mail order and helped establish that the obscure cartridge had genuinely been released. The game’s existence was not widely documented for many years. A copy discovered at a Cincinnati rummage sale in 2007 became the subject of discussion among Atari collectors, who worked to identify its developer and establish whether it was an authentic commercial release. A surviving advertisement found in Christianity Today in 2011 provided important evidence that the game had been marketed in 1983. Heritage describes the title as one of the rarest commercially released console games ever produced. However, estimates of how many cartridges were made vary among historical accounts, so the precise size of the original production run remains difficult to establish.The 2007 discovery was significant because Red Sea Crossing had largely disappeared from public knowledge. The game was not part of Atari’s mainstream catalogue, and its mail-order distribution meant that comparatively few examples were documented by collectors. After the cartridge was found, members of the Atari community investigated its origins and connected it to Steve Schustack. Historical accounts identify Schustack as the programmer and describe the game as an independent project released through Inspirational Video Concepts. The discovery eventually led to renewed interest in the game and to the appearance of additional examples. One copy sold at auction in 2012 for $10,400, while another copy that surfaced in Philadelphia was also sold that year. The earlier sales helped establish Red Sea Crossing as a sought-after rarity among Atari collectors.The Heritage lot consisted of the Atari 2600 cartridge and an accompanying cassette. The auction house described the cassette as particularly notable because it was the first time the tape itself had been presented at auction. That distinction matters because the cassette was part of the game’s original package but has been much less frequently documented than the cartridge. The game’s historical descriptions consistently mention the colouring book and audio recording, but surviving examples of the complete package are considerably harder to trace than reproductions and loose cartridges. Heritage described both items in the lot as being in excellent condition. The cartridge and cassette were nevertheless sold untested and as-is, with no returns.Heritage Auctions listed the item as lot 28003 in its 2026 Video Games Signature Auction. The auction took place on June 12 and 13, with the Red Sea Crossing lot recorded as sold on June 12 for $6,562.50. Heritage’s listing records 36 bids and registered phone bidders, with a 25% buyer’s premium applying to the lot. The result adds a new chapter to the history of a game that was originally sold through a single religious-magazine advertisement, rediscovered at a garage sale and later recognised as one of the most elusive Atari 2600 releases. The 2026 sale was especially notable not simply because of the cartridge’s rarity, but because it brought an original accompanying cassette into the auction record for the first time.
Article Summary: Red sea crossing was released for the atari 2600 in 1983 by inspirational video concepts. Unlike many commercial console games of the period, it was not distributed through ordinary retail channels. The game’s existence was not widely documented for many years.

Article Title: In 2007, Scottish cyclist Mark Beaumont left Paris to race around Earth; 194 days and 17 hours later, crashes, theft and exhaustion had not stopped him
Article Text:
Scottish adventurer Mark Beaumont is pictured during his long-distance cycling career and carrying the Olympic torch during the London Olympics torch relay. Beaumont carried the flame across the Forth Road Bridge in Scotland. Credits - Wikipedia

A path through hardship

Mark Beaumont cycles alongside a local rider and a donkey-drawn cart in eastern Pakistan during his 2007–08 record-setting journey around the world by bicycle. Credits - Wikipedia

Rewriting the record

Long before ultra-endurance sport became a global spectacle, crossing the world on two wheels was the domain of the odd and the dreamer. Record keepers had been tracking efforts at this achievement for decades, and the bar kept moving as riders pushed further into the unknown with little more than paper maps, panniers and persistence. A young man from rural Fife, a man who had spent his childhood cycling throughout Scotland for enjoyment, stepped into that bloodline in the summer of 2007. What came next would see him become one of the defining figures in endurance riding and rewrite what people thought was physically feasible on a bicycle.On 5 August 2007, Mark Beaumont left the Arc de Triomphe in Paris on a laden touring bike with an objective that appeared almost reckless for someone who had never attempted anything on this scale before. He planned to ride about 100 miles a day, alone and unsupported, until he had travelled round the globe and got back to where he started. His bicycle, a Koga Miyata with a Rohloff internal gear hub, was loaded with around 30 kilogrammes of tools, spare parts and video equipment, since he was chronicling the voyage himself for what would become a BAFTA nominated BBC film. Cycling UK , the membership club that has long backed British riders on just this sort of personal endeavour, later published his own report of how three years of planning went into that single departure from Paris.Beaumont’s journey carried him east via Europe and Russia, through Central Asia and the Indian subcontinent, across Southeast Asia and Australia, and then across North America before one more trans-Atlantic trip back to France. It was a tough trail, and preparation wouldn’t make it easier. In Lafayette, Louisiana, he was hit by a car and robbed later that same day, an experience that would have killed most people’s endeavours on the spot. Elsewhere he fought illness and the sort of physical disintegration that comes from sixteen or more hours a day in the saddle for months on end without rest. He’d also meant to be a vegetarian but had little choice but to give that up during the ride simply to keep enough calories going in to survive the daily mileage.It’s not only the distance but also the isolation that makes the achievement exceptional. Throughout the ride, Beaumont had no support car, no mechanic and no chef. If his gear broke or his body let him down, he had to tackle the problem himself, often in isolated parts of Pakistan, Iran or the Australian outback where help was hours or days away. He used paper maps in an age when smartphone navigation didn’t even exist for bikes and had his mother back home assist him in plotting alternative routes if roads were blocked.On 15 February 2008, Beaumont cycled back past the Arc de Triomphe, having completed almost 18,000 miles in 194 days and 17 hours. That broke the previous world record by 81 days, a margin so vast that even veteran endurance athletes who had thought the mark would stand for years were startled. His accomplishment was officially validated, and the lineage of riders who chased and ultimately beat his time is still recorded on the official Guinness World Records page for the quickest circumnavigation by bicycle. Other cyclists would eventually beat Beaumont's own record, such as Vin Cox in 2010, before Beaumont himself recaptured the supported version of the championship in 2017 with a specially organised support squad, further lowering his own original time.But it is the 2007 solo ride that attracted public attention, because he did it without a safety net. Beaumont then returned to his old university, the University of St Andrews , to speak to students about the trip. He didn't frame it as some prank, but as proof that ordinary preparedness, stubbornness and a tolerance for discomfort might take a person further than nearly anyone expected. The ride raised £18,000 for charity and he utilised the platform it established to launch a series of additional expeditions including the length of the Americas trip from Alaska to Argentina and a solo unsupported crossing from Cairo to Cape Town.Nearly two decades later, Beaumont's original circumnavigation is still cited as a moment when unsupported round-the-world cycling moved from an oddity to a recognised branch of endurance sport, inspiring later solo riders like Jenny Graham and a wave of amateur cyclists who attempt similar routes every year. It’s not just the miles that keep the story alive, but what it said about the extremes individuals will reach when curiosity and discipline collide.

Article Title: In 2010, an Irishman began running around the world; four years and roughly 50,000 km later, he finished a global route few runners had ever completed
Article Text:
Torres del Paine in Patagonia, a region Mangan crossed during his 50,000-km world run | Wikimedia Commons

The Dublin Marathon was only the starting point

50,000 km across 41 countries

The final stretch became a race against the clock

Dublin, Ireland, where Tony Mangan began and ended his four-year, 50,000-km run around the world | Wikimedia Commons

He finished where the journey began

Tony Mangan started the Dublin Marathon on October 25, 2010, kept running, and began a journey that would take him across five continents, six deserts and 41 countries before he returned to Dublin four years later. The World Runners Association records his completed route at 50,000 km over 1,461 days, and lists it as the longest circumnavigation of the Earth on foot under its records.Mangan had spent years thinking about running around the world, and eventually turned the idea into what he called his “World Jog”, starting with the 2010 Dublin Marathon. He continued westward across Ireland to Dunquin, the westernmost point of the Dingle Peninsula, after completing the race.Mangan crossed North America, moved through Central and South America, continued through Australia and Asia, and eventually returned to Europe. The World Runners Association’s route record lists sections through Canada, the United States, Panama, Colombia, Argentina, New Zealand, Australia, Indonesia and Turkey before the final European leg back to Dublin. Mangan averaged roughly the equivalent of a marathon a day during the journey, and also travelled with a small running buggy called Nirvana, which carried equipment including clothing, food and camping gear.The Irish Independent reported that he had already covered 50,000 km and crossed five continents, six deserts and 41 countries in September 2014. He had begun his return through Europe after completing the long sections across the Americas, Australasia and Asia.Mangan encountered extreme conditions along the way, including severe heat and cold, and his own account of the expedition describes dehydration in Mexico, temperatures that reached minus 30C in the United States and storms in Patagonia. He also ran across the Australian outback.The World Runners Association records that Mangan undertook the 50,000-km run for Aware, which is an Irish organisation working in the area of depression. The run therefore combined his long-standing ambition to circumnavigate the world with fundraising and public awareness.By the time Mangan reached Europe, the expedition was already approaching its fourth year. He had accumulated tens of thousands of kilometres on the road, but the final distance still required him to keep running through Ireland before returning to the Dublin Marathon where the journey had begun.In September 2014, the Irish Independent reported that Mangan was completing the last part of his journey through Ireland after returning from abroad. He had already reached approximately 50,000 km, but continued running until the expedition formally ended with the Dublin Marathon. The final race gave the journey a fixed finishing point rather than ending somewhere along the road.On October 27, 2014, Mangan crossed the Dublin Marathon finish line in 6:08:30, completing the final stage of a journey that had started with the same race four years earlier. The Irish Independent reported that he had covered roughly 50,000 km by the time he finished.Mangan returned to Ireland in September 2014 and spent the final weeks completing a roughly 1,600-km circuit of the country. He then entered the Dublin Marathon on October 27, four years after the race that had started his world run.The Irish Independent reported that Mangan crossed the Dublin Marathon finish line in 6:08:30, and brought the journey to an end after approximately 50,000 km. The finish was not at the same point where he had first crossed the line in 2010 by accident; rather, it was deliberate, since Dublin had been both the beginning and the endpoint of the route. The World Runners Association currently lists the completed run at 50,000 km and 1,461 days and identifies Mangan as holding its longest-circumnavigation record.
Article Summary: Tony mangan started the dublin marathon on october 25, 2010. He continued running across five continents, six deserts and 41 countries. The world runners association records his completed route at 50,000 km over 1,461 days. He returned to ireland in september 2014 and spent the final weeks completing a roughly 1,600-km circuit of the country.
